It is the first medical prescription in Japanese myth, and the deed that marks the future land-master out from his rivals. The Ordeals Below: The Trials of Ne-no-Kuni Fleeing his brothers' repeated attempts to kill him, Ōnamuji descends to Ne-no-Kuni, the root-land of Susanoo, as the Kojiki (Book I) relates. There he loves Susanoo's daughter Suseribime, and the storm-god tests him: a night in a hall of snakes, a night in a hall of centipedes and wasps — each survived through Suseribime's protective scarves — and a burning meadow where a mouse leads him to safety underground and retrieves the arrow Susanoo had fired. When Ōnamuji at last washes the great god's hair and steals away with Suseribime, Susanoo's sword, bow and heavenly lute, the pursuing god yields and proclaims him Ōkuninushi-no-kami, Great Land-Master, bidding him drive out his brothers and rule the land. Nation-Builders: The Dwarf from Across the Sea While Ōkuninushi labours to order the land, the Kojiki (Book I) tells, a tiny god arrives across the waves in a skiff of kagami pod-husks, wearing the skin of a moth: Sukunabikona, son of the great producer Kamimusubi (the Nihon Shoki variants name Takamimusubi). The two make and consolidate the land together, and devise the arts of medicine and protective magic for gods, men and beasts. When the work is done, Sukunabikona departs for Tokoyo no kuni, the far land beyond the sea, leaving Ōkuninushi to guard the realm they built. The Great Abdication: Kuni-yuzuri — the Transfer of the Land When Amaterasu resolves that her line shall rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains, the Kojiki (Book I; cf. the Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods scrolls) records that the warrior-god Takemikazuchi is sent to Izumo, where he thrusts his sword into the shore and demands Ōkuninushi's answer. The land-master defers to his sons: Kotoshironushi consents at once, while Ajisuki-takahikone resists and is subdued in a divine wrestling-bout. Ōkuninushi then cedes the land — on terms: a grand palace is to be built for him with pillars raised high and crossbeams thick, and his worship is to be perpetuated by the heavenly line itself. That promised palace is Izumo no Ōyashiro, the Grand Shrine of Izumo, and the treaty-in-myth is remembered as kuni-yuzuri. Syncretism: Japan's gods met no Roman pantheon; Ōkuninushi's later travels ran through Buddhism instead. Through the folk reading Daikoku-sama of the characters 大国, he was identified with Daikokuten , the Japanese form of Mahākāla, becoming the smiling god of wealth and the household hearth — one of the Seven Gods of Fortune. At Izumo the older identity survived intact: there he remains the great matchmaker of en-musubi , the binding of marriage fates, and in the month the rest of Japan calls Kannazuki, 'the godless month', Izumo calls it Kami-ari-zuki — 'the month the gods are here', when the eight million kami convene at his shrine. Cultural legacy: Ōkuninushi still anchors the Izumo region of Shimane, where Izumo-taisha draws millions of pilgrims and couples across Japan pray to him as the nation's matchmaker. The white hare of Inaba endures as the emblem of Tottori prefecture, and his son Kotoshironushi presides over the great pilgrimage shrine of Kotohira in Shikoku. The word kuni-yuzuri itself remains the standard term for the peaceful cession of sovereignty — the god's abdication absorbed into the political vocabulary of Japan. Extended meditation: The Ōkuninushi cycle is a treaty written as myth. The 8th-century mythographers of the Yamato court preserved, almost lovingly, a rival sovereignty — an earth-line descended from Susanoo that owned the visible world — and then sanctified its surrender to the sun-line of Amaterasu. What Ōkuninushi received in exchange is telling: not power but cult, the towering shrine and the empire's perpetual worship. He is therefore the god of everything the heavenly line does not do — healing, farming, matchmaking, the pragmatic order of the reed-plain. Many scholars read the cycle as encoding real negotiations between Yamato and the old Izumo region; whether charter or memory, it makes Ōkuninushi the most humane of sovereigns: a ruler who learned kingship through ordeals beneath the earth, and who gave up his kingdom so that his land — and his god — could endure.

The Third Voice of Delphi: Titaness of Prophecy, Keeper of the Oracle before Apollo Phoíbē is the Titaness of prophecy , the 'shining one' whose name is simply the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright'. Before Apollo ever spoke at Delphi, the Pythia's own prayer names her the oracle's third keeper — after Gaia and Themis — who passed the seat to her grandson as a birthday gift. She is light as foresight : the radiance that sees before it shines. The Oracular Seat: Aeschylus gives Delphi’s succession as Earth, then Themis, then Phoíbē — who yields the seat to Apollo as a birthday gift (Eumenides 1–8). Prophetic Light: Her name is the feminine of Phoîbos, “the bright one” — the shining, prophetic power she hands down to her grandson. The Golden Line: Daughter of Ouranos and Gaia, wife of Koios, mother of Lētō — grandmother of Apollo and Ártemis (Theogony 404–410). Symbols: Golden Crown — Hesiod's sole epithet for her in the Titan catalogue — Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον, 'Phoebe of the golden crown' (Theogony 136): the royalty of the eldest generation, and light worn on the brow.; Delphic Tripod — The Pythia's three-legged seat at Delphi, which Aeschylus' succession makes hers third, after Gaia and Themis (Eumenides 1–8) — the one concrete object to which her mythic tenure attaches.; Omphalos — The navel-stone marking Delphi as the center of the world; part of the sanctuary landscape of the oracle she held and handed on. She has no independent iconography — her attributes are Delphi's.; Laurel — The prophetic tree of Delphi, inherited by Apollo together with the seat she gave him; with her it marks the continuity of the shrine rather than a personal emblem.; Prophetic Radiance — Her name itself — the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright, shining' — is her symbol: light understood as foresight, the gleam that sees ahead.; The Moon — A late association: Roman poets use Phoebē as a name of the moon paired with Phoebus the sun, and through her granddaughter Artemis she drifts lunar. Ancient, but poetic rather than cultic. Phoíbē stands quietly at the hinge of Greek myth: a Titan of the eldest generation whose role is to inherit and to hand on — the oracle to Apollo, the bloodline to Leto. Her myths are genealogies that glow: everything she touches passes light forward. Hesiod: Golden-Crowned among the Titans In the Theogony (132–136), Hesiod catalogues the twelve Titans born to Ouranos and Gaia — Ocean, Koios, Krios, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rheia, Themis, Mnemosyne, Tethys, and Kronos — and among them 'Phoíbē of the golden crown' (Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον). She is one of the few in the list to carry an epithet at all, and hers is an epithet of light. Hesiod records no deed of hers; the eldest Titans are not actors but origins, the generation from which the Olympian world descends. Hesiod: The Much-Desired Couch of Koios Later in the Theogony (404–410), Phoíbē 'ascended the much-desired couch of Koios' (Φοίβη δ' αὖ Κοίου πολυήρατον ἷξε λέχος εἰσαναβᾶσα) and conceived Leto — 'dark-robed, gentle, the mildest of all who dwell on Olympus'. The line continues without pause: Leto bears 'Apollo and arrow-pouring Artemis' to Zeus ( Theogony 918–920), so Phoíbē stands at the head of the Delphic family, grandmother to the two Olympians of light. Hesiod gives the marriage no quarrel and no story beyond the bed and the child; for a Titaness of the first generation, the genealogy is the myth. Aeschylus: The Third Voice of Delphi The opening lines of Aeschylus' Eumenides (1–8) preserve her greatest role. The Pythia, praying at Delphi, names Gaia 'first of prophets' and Themis second upon her mother's seat; third — 'with her consent, and by no violence' — sat 'another Titan, a child of Earth, Phoíbē'. Phoíbē then gave the throne to Apollo 'as a birthday gift' (γενέθλιον δόσιν), 'and he bears his name Phoíbos as a namesake from hers' (τὸ Φοίβης δ' ὄνομ' ἔχει παρώνυμον). It is the only peaceful succession in the violent history of the Greek gods: the oracle changes hands as a family inheritance, and the new god's famous epithet is, the tragedian insists, simply his grandmother's name. Apollodorus: Two Daughters of Prophecy Apollodorus ( Library 1.4.1) gives her motherhood its full shape: from Koios and Phoíbē spring two daughters, Asteria and Leto. Asteria, 'the starry one', bears Hekátē to Perses ( Theogony 409–412), the torch-bearing goddess of crossroads whom Zeus honors above all; Leto bears Apollo and Artemis. Through one daughter flows the lineage of night sky and moonlight, through the other the lineage of sunlit prophecy: both of Delphi's lights, in effect, are Phoíbē's grandchildren. Syncretism: Phoíbē never received a Roman cult of her own; Rome met her inside Apollo, whose Greek epithet Phoebus became a standard poetic name — and whose name Aeschylus had already declared to be hers (Eumenides 7–8). In Latin poetry the feminine Phoebē then hardens into a name of the moon itself, paired with Phoebus the sun, so the Titaness survives in Rome as a word rather than a worship. Through her granddaughter Artemis–Diana, later poets quietly fold her into the lunar goddess, but the equation remains poetic, never cultic, and no ancient author confuses the two genealogies. Cultural legacy: The name lives on in English as Phoebe — entering the Christian tradition through Phoíbē of Cenchreae, the deaconess Paul commends to the Roman church (Romans 16:1) — and it has been one of the most durable classical given names in the language ever since. Astronomy keeps the Titaness herself: Phoebe , the dark retrograde outer moon of Saturn discovered by W. H. Pickering in 1899, is named for her, a fitting moon for the Titaness of light. And whenever literature writes 'Phoebus Apollo', it repeats — whether it knows it or not — her name, which Aeschylus says Apollo took from his grandmother. The small American flycatcher called the phoebe, by contrast, is named for its call: a false friend, not a descendant. Extended meditation: Phoíbē is nearly invisible in Greek worship, and that invisibility is the point: her significance is structural rather than devotional. She is the lawful transmission of prophecy. In a myth-world built on violent succession — Ouranos castrated by Kronos, Kronos overthrown by Zeus — Aeschylus makes hers the sole peaceful one: the oracle passes 'with consent and by no violence', as a gift, and even leaves its name behind as a family inheritance. The Greeks seem to have felt that foresight, unlike kingship, could not be seized; it had to be bequeathed. Her shining is therefore not the blaze of the sun but the quiet lamp of knowledge kept burning across generations — from Earth, through law in Themis, through her, into Apollo's daylight.

The Uninvited: Goddess of Strife and Discord — the quarrel that topples kingdoms and the rivalry that builds them Éris is strife personified — the quarrel, the feud, the rivalry that Greeks both cursed and quietly praised. Born of Nyx, Night herself , she is the one goddess who was never asked to the feast and who therefore changed the world. Yet Hesiod insists there are two Erises : the hateful one who sows war, and the praiseworthy one who stirs even the idle to work. She is the most honest deity in the pantheon — the Greeks' name for a force they could not escape and could not entirely disown. The Golden Apple: Uninvited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, she rolls the golden apple “for the fairest” — the first cause of the Trojan War (Cypria). The Two Erises: Hesiod separates the hateful Strife from her elder sister, the good Eris who stirs idle men to work (Works and Days 11–26). The War-Stirrer: In the Iliad she walks the battle small at first, her head striking the sky as she delights in the din (Iliad 4.440–443). Symbols: The Golden Apple — The apple of the Hesperides that Éris rolled among the wedding guests of Peleus and Thetis; the Cypria tradition (preserved in Proclus' summary) makes it the seed of the Trojan War — a single piece of fruit as the first cause of the greatest war in Greek memory.; The Inscription 'Kallistēi' — 'For the fairest' (τῇ καλλίστῃ) — the words cut into the apple itself. The inscription, not the fruit, is the weapon: a superlative with three claimants is a quarrel engineered in miniature.; Viper-Tressed Hair — Virgil gives the Roman Discordia serpent-entwined locks bound with blood-drenched fillets (Aeneid 6.280, 'Discordia demens, vipereum crinem vittis innexa cruentis'), kin to the Furies — strife wearing the visual grammar of vengeance.; The Swelling Stature — In Iliad 4 (440–445) Éris is 'small at first, but then she fixes her head in heaven while her feet walk the earth' — her growing body is her emblem: discord is always born tiny.; Place beside Árēs — Homer calls her 'sister and companion of man-slaying Ares' (Iliad 4.441), and on the shield of Achilles she strides through battle beside Tumult and Doom, clutching the wounded and the dead (Iliad 18.535–540). Her attribute is her company. Éris has no temples and almost no cult — her mythology is her meaning. Every surviving story is an anatomy of strife itself: where it comes from, whom it feeds, and how it grows. Genealogy: Born of Night, Mother of Calamities In the Theogony (224–232) Hesiod makes Éris a child of Nyx, Night, who bears her without father among the other dark abstractions — Death, Sleep, Blame, Woe. Éris then breeds her own terrible brood, the Kakodaimones: Toil (Ponos), Forgetfulness, Famine, Pains, Combats, Battles, Murders, Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lies , Disputes, Lawlessness, Ruin (Atē), and Oath, who 'troubles most of all men on earth when anyone deliberately swears falsely'. The genealogy is a single claim stated plainly: from one quarrel, every misery descends . The Two Erises: Hesiod's Correction The Works and Days (11–26) opens by amending the poet's own Theogony: 'there was not one kind of Strife after all — on earth there are two .' The first, the elder, men blame, for she 'fosters evil war and slaughter'. The second, whom Zeus set in the roots of the earth, is much better for mortals : she rouses even the shiftless to work, for 'potter rivals potter, carpenter carpenter; beggar envies beggar, and poet poet'. Here Éris is split in two — envy as destroyer and emulation as the engine of all human striving — one of the earliest pieces of moral reflection in Greek literature. The Wedding Feast: The Golden Apple of the Hesperides At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, all the gods were feasted — except Éris, whose very nature barred her from the invitation list. The Cypria , as summarized in Proclus' Chrestomathy , tells that she came anyway and threw among the guests a golden apple 'to be a prize of beauty', inscribed kallistēi — 'for the fairest' . Hera, Athēnâ, and Aphrodítē each claimed it; the dispute was sent for judgment to Paris on Mount Ida, and from that judgment, Proclus says flatly, came the Trojan War. Hyginus ( Fabulae 92) retells the same scene. It is the founding myth of discord: exclusion breeds the quarrel that topples a kingdom . On the Battlefield: Small at First, Then Filling the Sky Homer's most haunting personification of war comes in Iliad 4 (440–445), as the two armies close: among them walks Éris, 'the sister and companion of man-slaying Ares — she rears only a small crest at first, but then she fixes her head in the heavens while her feet walk the earth', hurling bitterness into the midst of both hosts. She reappears on the shield of Achilles ( Iliad 18.535–540), bloody-robed among the wounded and the dead. The image is precise: discord begins as a murmur and ends with its head in the clouds — and once she stands, no god can pull her down. Syncretism: Rome adopted her as Discordia , and the Roman poets made her darker still. Ennius opened his account of the outbreak of the Second Punic War with her: 'Discordia taetra belli ferratos postis portasque refregit' — 'when foul Discord burst the iron-bound posts and gates of war' ( Annales , fr. 225 Skutsch), an image Virgil deliberately echoes at the underworld's entrance in Aeneid 6.280, where Discordia demens stands with viper-entwined, blood-bound hair. She never acquired the civic cult that other translations did — Rome, like Greece, preferred to name strife rather than worship it. Her modern afterlife is stranger and more literal than most: the Discordian movement of the 1960s made her its patroness, and in 2006 the dwarf planet whose discovery provoked the reclassification of Pluto was formally named Eris — a fitting tribute, the IAU noted, to the goddess of strife and discord. Cultural legacy: Her Roman name survives everywhere in English: discord, discordant, discordance , and the idiom ' apple of discord ' for the object of a quarrel — a phrase that walked straight out of the Cypria into the modern tongues of Europe. Discordianism's Principia Discordia canonized her as the counter-goddess of an orderly world, and the dwarf planet Eris carries her name in every astronomy textbook, so the 'tenth planet' that demoted Pluto keeps her quarrel alive in the heavens. Among the Olympian circle she remains what she always was: the goddess nobody worships and everybody obeys. Extended meditation: Éris exposes something unusual about Greek religious thought: its willingness to personify what it disapproved of . She has essentially no cult — no sanctuary, no festival, no priesthood — yet the poets cannot write a war without her. Hesiod's two Erises show the tradition arguing with itself: strife is the curse of mankind and, simultaneously, the condition of every human excellence, for without rivalry the potter never improves his pot. The apple myth extends the insight into politics: the quarrel was not caused by wickedness but by a superlative, by the mere existence of 'fairest' among three goddesses. To the Greeks, Éris was less a villain than a diagnosis — the recognition that conflict is not an interruption of the cosmic order but one of its permanent residents, daughter of the Night that precedes all things.

The Blooming Muse: Comedy, Idyll, Good Cheer Tháleia is the Muse of comedy and idyllic poetry , one of the nine daughters Zeus fathered on Mnémosynē. Her name is the Greek word for flourishing — from θάλλω, 'to bloom' — and in the plural, θαλίαι, it means nothing less than festivities: the good cheer of the feast. The Greeks gave laughter a Muse, and they named her Blooming. The Comic Mask: Her standing attribute in ancient art — the laughing face of the theater, held lightly in one hand. The Shepherd's Staff: The crook of bucolic song, the green world of shepherds and idylls she was said to guard. The Green Shoot: The θαλλός her name proclaims: fresh growth, festivity, the year turning toward abundance. Symbols: Comic mask — Her defining attribute in ancient iconography — laughter given a face; Shepherd's staff (pedum) — The bucolic world of idyllic poetry: flocks, shade, and song; Ivy wreath — The plant of Dionysos, god of the theater where comedy was performed; Comic slipper (soccus) — The low shoe of comic actors, set against tragedy's high cothurnus; Frame drum — The tambourine of the Corybantes, the ecstatic dancers said to be her sons Tháleia rarely acts alone: her myths are the myths of the Muses as a body. What the sources give us is her birth, her name, and one startling marriage — to Apollo, father of her dancing sons. Theogony: Nine Nights, Nine Daughters Hesiod tells how Mnémosynē, Memory herself, lay with Zeus for nine nights and bore the nine Muses 'to be a forgetting of evils and a rest from cares' ( Theogony 53–62). When he names them, Tháleia stands third: 'Kleiṓ and Eutérpē and Tháleia and Melpoménē' ( Theogony 76–79). From the beginning, then, laughter and festivity are numbered among the daughters of Memory — comedy is not beneath remembrance but one of its gifts. Iliad: The Silencing of Thamyris In Iliad 2 (594–600), the Catalogue of Ships pauses at Dōrion, where the Thracian singer Thamyris was stopped on his way from Oichalia. He had boasted he would outsing the Muses themselves; in their anger they maimed him, 'took away his divine song, and made him forget his lyre-playing.' The Muses act here as one undivided power — Tháleia among them — and their punishment is the precise opposite of their gift: not forgetting of cares, but forgetting of song. Apollodorus: Mother of the Corybantes Apollodorus records that 'from Thaleia and Apollo were born the Corybantes' ( Bibliotheca 1.3.4) — the ecstatic, armed dancers who clash their shields around the mountain mother. The notice is late and quietly astonishing: the Muse of comedy wed to the god of measure and the lyre, and their children are wild percussion and dance. Perhaps the genealogy knows something true — that laughter, music, and ecstatic motion are nearer kin than the genres pretend. The Other Tháleia: A Grace of the Same Name The name flowers twice in Hesiod. A few hundred lines after the Muses, he names the Chárites born to Zeus and the Oceanid Eurýnomē: 'Aglaía and Euphrosýnē and lovely Thaleía' ( Theogony 907–911). Pausanias (9.35) confirms that the cities of Greece disagreed about the Graces' names and number, and that Thaleia's place among them was old. The duplication is no scribal error: blooming belongs both to song and to grace, and Greek theology let one word keep both houses. Syncretism: Rome adopted the nine Musae almost without translation, and Thalia kept her Greek name; it was in late antique and Renaissance iconography that she was fixed once and for all as comedy's patron, mask in hand, one of the paired faces of the theater. Her namesake the Charis lived a parallel afterlife as one of the three Graces of Western art — Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia, the dancers of Botticelli's Primavera . Through her collective she passes into the very words 'music' and 'museum,' both children of the Greek Mousa . Cultural legacy: No common English noun descends from Tháleia's name alone — her legacy travels under other flags. She presides in spirit over Theocritus's Idylls , the bucolic poems that gave English the word 'idyll' for every scene of pastoral peace. Theaters bear her name — Hamburg's Thalia Theater most famously — and the paired masks of comedy and tragedy that still sign for the stage are, by long convention, hers and Melpoménē's. As a given name, Thalia has never gone out of use; the Muse of laughter is one of the few Greek deities people still name their daughters after. Extended meditation: Honesty requires a caveat: Hesiod assigns no spheres to the Muses. The tidy division — Tháleia for comedy, Melpoménē for tragedy, Kalliṓpē for epic — is a Hellenistic and Roman codification, unknown to the archaic sources, which treat the nine as one undivided choir. Yet the later assignment is not arbitrary decoration. That comedy receives a Muse at all is the telling fact: the Greeks did not rank laughter beneath song but placed both in the care of Memory's daughters, performed together at the festivals of Dionysos. Her name carries the argument further. Θάλλω is what the green world does in spring — and in the plural, θαλίαι is what the feast does in winter. One root holds vegetation and celebration together, as if the Greeks suspected that festivity is simply abundance made audible. A Muse named Blooming says that comedy is not escape from the serious world but its renewal: the year, and the city, flowering again.

The Breath of Spring: The West Wind, Gentlest of the Anemoi Zéphyros is the west wind of the Greeks — the mildest of the four Anemoi, the breeze that loosens winter and calls up the flowers. Where Bóreas rages and Nótos drowns ships in rain, Zéphyros is the wind the poets loved: the steady, fruit-bearing breath that fans the orchards of the blessed and carries spring north into the human world. Herald of Spring: Gentlest of the Anemoi, his west wind loosens winter’s grip and brings the swallow season home. Father of Swift Horses: With the harpy Podarge he sires Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal, wind-swift horses of Achilles (Iliad 16.148–151). Bridegroom of Flora: Roman poets wed him to Flora; Ovid lets her recall she was the nymph Chloris until Zéphyros took her as his bride (Fasti 5.195–212). Symbols: Garland of Flowers — On the Tower of the Winds in Athens, Zéphyros is carved as a youth whose folded cloak spills blossoms — his spring-bearing nature made visible in stone.; Wings — Like all the Anemoi, he is winged in Greek and Roman art; the winds fly, and their wings mark them as powers of the air rather than ordinary gods.; Swift Horses — By Pódargē the harpy he fathered Xánthos and Bálios, the immortal horses of Achilles — the wind's own speed given equine form.; The Swallow — The swallow's return was proverbially bound to the west wind's season; both were the first messengers that winter had broken.; Billowing Sail — A kind wind for sailors: steady, mild, and western — the breeze that fills canvas without violence and carries ships home.; Youthful Bloom — In art he appears as a beautiful, unbearded youth, a wind conceived not as a destroyer but as a lover — fitting the bridegroom of Chlōris. Zéphyros is a minor god with an outsized poetic life: born of Dawn, lover of flowers, father of the fastest horses ever to run. His myths are few but luminous — each one binds the west wind to speed, desire, and the returning spring. Birth of the Winds: Son of Dawn and the Starry Sky In Theogony 378–380, Hesiod records that Eōs (Dawn) bore to Astraios, the starry dusk, the mighty winds: Zéphyros , Bóreas , and Nótos — 'a goddess lying in love with a god'. The genealogy is exact: the clearing west wind is the child of first light and the star-field, born at the seam where night opens into day. Iliad: Father of Achilles's Horses In Iliad 16 (149–151), Patroklos harnesses Achilles's immortal pair, Xánthos and Bálios, 'whom Pódargē, the harpy swift of foot, bore to Zéphyros the west wind as she grazed in a meadow beside the stream of Ōkeanos'. A wind coupling with a storm-snatcher in a meadow: Homer makes the horses' supernatural speed a literal inheritance. It is Xánthos, this same wind-begotten colt, who later speaks with a human voice to foretell Achilles's death ( Iliad 19, 404–417). Roman Flora: The Abduction of Chlōris In Ovid's Fasti 5 (195–214), the goddess Flora tells her own story: 'I who am now called Flora was once Chlōris… Zéphyros saw me, desired me, and carried me off' — then made her his lawful wife and gave her dominion over every flower, so that in her garden 'it is always spring'. Hyginus ( Fabulae ) preserves the fruit of the union: their son Karpós , 'Fruit' itself, the harvest that follows blossom. Odyssey: The Breeze of the Blessed Orchards In Odyssey 7 (112–132), the garden of King Alkinoös on Scheria — fruit upon fruit, pear ripening on pear, never failing winter or summer — is kept in perpetual bearing because 'the breath of Zéphyros , ever blowing, causes some fruits to swell and others to ripen'. Homer needs no allegory here: the west wind simply is the climate of paradise, the mildest air imaginable, made divine. Syncretism: The Romans called him Favōnius , from favēre , 'to favor' — the propitious wind — and married him to their own flower-goddess Flōra, whose festival, the Floralia, kept the Greek Chlōris-marriage alive in cult. Horace ( Odes 1.4) sings winter loosening 'under the welcome west wind', and Virgil lets Favonius breathe through the Georgics as the air that unbinds the fields. Through Latin poetry the name passed intact into every European vernacular: the gentle west wind of Greece became the zephyr of the modern world. Cultural legacy: English zephyr — 'a soft, gentle breeze' — descends directly from his name through Latin zephyrus , and has been a staple of English verse since Chaucer opened the Canterbury Tales with 'Zephirus… with his sweete breeth' quickening the spring crops. The word also gave its name to a fine, light yarn and to anything featherweight. Few Greek wind-gods survive so completely: not as a character, but as the very word English reaches for when the air turns kind. Extended meditation: The Greeks did not usually worship the winds with temples and myths of their own — they felt them, and feeling was enough. Zéphyros is the clearest case of a natural force crossing into personality precisely because it was pleasant : the storm winds stay brute daimones, but the wind that opens the flowers earned a wife, a marriage bed, and children. His ambivalence is quiet but real — the same wind that breeds Achilles's immortal horses also breeds the speed that carries the hero toward death. For the Greeks the west wind was proof that the divine could be gentle without ceasing to be power: a daimon you pray to by opening the orchard gate.

The Most Just of Centaurs: Wisdom · Teaching · Heroes Cheírōn is the exception among the wild κένταυροι : the immortal son of Kronos who dwells in a cave on Mount Pelion and turns raw princes into heroes. Where his kin are drunkards and rapine, Homer calls him δικαιότατος Κενταύρων — the most just of centaurs. He is the teacher: medicine for Asklepios , the lyre and the remedies for Achilles , the whole heroic craft for Iason and Herakles. The Tutor's Craft: He reared Achilles, Iásōn, and Asklepios on Mount Pēlion — “the most just of the Centaurs” (Iliad 11.832). The Healing Hand: He taught Asklepios the art of drugs, and was himself struck by Herakles’ hydra-venomed arrow that no healing art could cure. The Hunter's Art: From him the heroes learned the chase itself — tracking, coursing, and spear-work in the mountain wilds. Symbols: The Pelian Ash Spear — The great spear of ash wood that Cheírōn cut on Pelion's peak and gave to Peleus at his wedding — the same spear Achilles alone could wield (Iliad 16.143–144). The teacher's gift that arms the hero.; The Cave on Mount Pelion — His dwelling and school, the legendary academy of heroes where the gods themselves celebrated the wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Pindar, Pythian 9.29–30).; The Lyre — The instrument of the education he gave Achilles, who in Iliad 9 (186–189) is found in his hut singing the glories of heroes to the lyre.; Herbs and Remedies (φάρμακα) — The healing lore he taught Asklepios and gave to Peleus's line; Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave his father' (Iliad 4.219, 11.831–832).; The Hydra-Poisoned Arrow — Herakles's stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, that struck his knee and gave the immortal an unhealable wound (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).; The Stars — Zeus set him in the sky — remembered as Centaurus or Sagittarius — after he surrendered his immortality and died (Ovid, Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). Cheírōn stands at the hinge of two orders: Titan-born yet honored by the Olympians, beast-bodied yet the very image of wisdom. His myths are the myths of transmission — what one generation hands to the next. Birth: Son of Kronos and Philyra Kronos lay with the Oceanid Philyra in the shape of a horse, and from that union was born a child of double nature — half god, half horse: Apollodorus, Library 1.2.4. Pindar likewise names him the son of Philyra and Kronos, making Cheírōn the half-brother of Zeus ( Pythian 4.102–103). Abandoned by his mother, who in shame was changed into a linden tree in later telling, he was reared by Apollo and Artemis, from whom he learned the arts he would pass on. Thus the wisest of teachers begins as the child of deception and rejection. The School of Pelion: Tutor of the Heroes Pindar gives the roll of his pupils: in his cave Cheírōn reared Iason , gentle-handed Asklepios , whom he taught the craft of remedies, and Achilles , whom he fed on the marrow of lions and wild boars to make him fierce ( Nemean 3.43–58). Homer twice seals the bond: Achilles carries remedies 'that Cheiron gave to his father in friendship' ( Iliad 4.218–219), and is the man 'whom Cheiron taught, the most just of the centaurs' — δικαιότατος Κενταύρων ( Iliad 11.831–832). Actaeon and Herakles also passed through his tutelage. In Pindar's grief for Hieron, the poet wishes Cheírōn still lived in his cave, that another healer might come to Sicily ( Pythian 3.1–7). The Gift: The Spear for Peleus When Peleus married the sea-goddess Thetis, the wedding feast was held on Pelion at Cheírōn's cave, and the centaur gave the bridegroom a spear of mountain ash cut from Pelion's peak ( Iliad 16.143–144). That spear passed to Achilles, and at Troy no other Achaean could wield it — Patroklos himself left it behind when he donned Achilles's armor, 'heavy, huge, and strong.' The teacher's gift thus runs through the whole Iliad : it is the one weapon that marks the hero he made. The marriage it honored also produced the child Cheírōn would raise. The Wound and the Stars: The Immortal Who Chose Death When Herakles fought the wild centaurs at the cave of Pholos, one of his arrows — tipped with the hydra's incurable venom — struck Cheírōn's knee ( Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4). The poison that the great healer had no remedy for burned in his own flesh; immortal, he could neither heal nor die. Sophocles remembers the shaft as the one 'wherewith Cheiron was struck' ( Trachiniae 714–716). At last he surrendered his immortality and was allowed to die, and Zeus set him among the stars — Ovid watches the father of heroes' education take his place in the sky ( Fasti 5.379–414; cf. Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). The teacher's last lesson is mortality itself. Syncretism: Rome changed Cheírōn least of all the Greek figures: he keeps his name as Chiron in Latin, too singular to be merged with any Italian power. What Rome absorbed was his catasterism — Latin poets and star-cataloguers fixed him in the sky, debating whether the Centaurus or the Sagittarius was his (Ovid, Fasti 5; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). In later tradition he remains the named exception among his kind: Dante makes him chief of the centaurs who guard the violent in Inferno 12, still 'Chiron, who nursed Achilles.' The word 'centaur' (κένταυρος) traveled into every European language, but Cheírōn travels as himself. Cultural legacy: His name lives in the sky: the minor planet 2060 Chiron , discovered in 1977 between Saturn and Uranus, was named for him and gave its class of objects — the centaurs , bodies orbiting among the giant planets — their collective name. Modern astrology adopted him as the emblem of the wounded healer , the one whose incurable hurt becomes the source of healing for others. Ancient herbalists named the plant centaury (κενταύριον, Centaurium) after the centaur's healing lore. And the old association of his name with χείρ, the hand, echoes — though by the word's own root, not by his name — in 'surgery,' from χειρουργία, 'hand-work.' Extended meditation: Cheírōn is the Greek answer to a question the centauromachy asks in stone at Olympia and on the Parthenon: can nature be educated? He is a κένταυρος — the very type of ungoverned appetite — who is instead called most just . That he is Kronos's son and Zeus's half-brother matters: he belongs to the older, Titan order, yet serves the new one by raising its heroes, as if the wild past could be redeemed only by becoming a teacher. His unhealable wound completes the thought — the master of remedies cannot master his own pain, and immortality becomes not a privilege but a sentence. That he must surrender deathlessness to find release is among the most quietly radical moments in Greek myth: even an immortal may long for the human portion.

Original script for Manannán: Manannán mac Lir Script: Medieval Irish (Latin script) Transliteration: Manannán mac Lir Steps: Old Irish was written in the Latin alphabet using Insular minuscule from the early medieval period. The name appears in the Ulster Cycle and Mythological Cycle as Manannán mac Lir, 'son of Lir (the sea)'. The acute accent on the final á marks a long vowel in modern scholarly convention. The Unicode restoration Manannán preserves the long vowel; the ASCII form flattens the name. Sources: [object Object], [object Object], [object Object]

Original script for Dažbog: Дажбог Script: Church Slavonic / East Slavic Cyrillic Transliteration: Dažbog Steps: The name is attested in East Slavic chronicles as Дажьбогъ (Dažĭbogŭ) and in the Primary Chronicle. It is usually analyzed as daždĭ 'rain, gift' + bogŭ 'god', hence 'giving god' or 'rain god'. The modern Unicode restoration Dažbog uses the caron ž; the medieval Cyrillic spelling includes the reduced jer vowels ь and ъ. The Cyrillic form is not registrable in .com; the Latin transliteration Dažbog is. Sources: [object Object], [object Object], [object Object]

Original script for Jizō: 地蔵 Script: Japanese Kanji (Jinmeiyō) Transliteration: Jizō Steps: Sanskrit Kṣitigarbha ('Earth Treasury' or 'Earth Womb') was translated into Chinese as 地藏 (Dìzàng). Japanese borrowed the compound as 地蔵, read in Sino-Japanese as Jizō. Hepburn romanisation writes the long vowel with a macron: Jizō. The ASCII form jizo loses the length mark, collapsing the distinction between short and long ō. The Unicode restoration Jizō is registrable in .com; the kanji form is not supported in the .com IDN table. Sources: [object Object], [object Object], [object Object]

Original script for Yām: 𐎊𐎎 Script: Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet Transliteration: ym Steps: Yammu is written ym 𐎊𐎎 throughout the Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) An earlier name-form yw 𐎊𐎆 appears at KTU 1.1 IV before his renaming to Yammu Syllabic cuneiform renders the name ᵈYa-a-mi (Emar); the logogram ᵈA.AB.BA (sea) also writes him at Ugarit Sources: KTU 1.1–1.6 (Baal Cycle), Yam (god), Wikipedia attestation summary

Original script for Pazuzu: 𒀭𒉺𒍪𒍪 Script: Cuneiform Transliteration: ᵈpa-zu-zu Steps: The standard spelling on Pazuzu heads and statues is ᵈpa-zu-zu, from Incantation A: anāku ᵈpa-zu-zu mār Ḫanbi, 'I am Pazuzu, son of Ḫanbi' A variant pa-su-su is also attested; the romanization 'pà.zu.zu' in some literature uses other signs and is not followed here Sources: Standard Pazuzu Incantation A (Wiggermann, Mesopotamian Protective Spirits), eScholarship Pazuzu corpus

Original script for Kingu: 𒀭𒆥𒄖 Script: Cuneiform Transliteration: ᵈqin-gu Steps: The most widespread spelling is ᵈqin-gu; sporadic variants dqi-in-gu, dqin-ga and dqin-gi occur (Krebernik, RlA 11) Modern scholarship prefers the form Qingu, of Sumerian origin Sources: Krebernik, RlA 11 s.v. Qingu, Enuma Elish

Original script for Lahmu: 𒀭𒌓𒈬 Script: Cuneiform Transliteration: ᵈlaḫ-mu Steps: Written ᵈlaḫ-mu in Enuma Elish I (Wiggermann 1992); the UD sign supplies the rare laḫ value Sources: Wiggermann, Mesopotamian Protective Spirits (1992), Enuma Elish I

Original script for Lahamu: 𒀭𒆷𒄩𒈬 Script: Cuneiform Transliteration: ᵈla-ḫa-mu Steps: Written ᵈla-ḫa-mu, paired with Lahmu in Enuma Elish I; the la-ḫa-mu reading is corroborated by quoted Akkadian lines Sources: Enuma Elish I

Original script for Tarḫunash: 𒀭𒌓 Script: Cuneiform (Hittite, logographic) Transliteration: ᵈU (also ᵈIŠKUR 𒀭𒅎, ᵈ10 𒀭𒌋) Steps: Hittite scribes almost always wrote the Storm-god logographically as ᵈU or ᵈIŠKUR (also ᵈ10) The underlying Hittite name Tarḫunna- is reconstructed from the Old Hittite attestation ᵈIŠKUR-un-ni (KBo 3.22 obv. 3); a fully syllabic Hittite spelling is not attested (Kloekhorst, EDHIL p. 835) Sources: Kloekhorst, EDHIL p. 835, KBo 3.22

Original script for Arinna: 𒀭𒌓 𒌷𒀀𒊑𒅔𒈾 Script: Cuneiform (Hittite, mixed logographic-syllabic) Transliteration: ᵈUTU ᵁᴿᵁa-ri-in-na Steps: The Sun goddess of Arinna is written ᵈUTU ᵁᴿᵁa-ri-in-na — the Sumerian sun logogram plus the syllabic town name 'Arinniti' ('the Arinnian') is an attested epithet; her phonetic Hittite name is unknown (Hattian Eštan, Hittite transcription Ištanu) Sources: Popko / Taracha via Sun goddess of Arinna scholarship
Original script for Telipinu: 𒀭𒋼𒂊𒇷𒁉𒉡𒌑 Script: Cuneiform (Hittite) Transliteration: ᵈte(-e)-li-pí-nu(-ú) Steps: Written ᵈte(-e)-li-pí-nu(-ú) (Beckman, RlA 13, 2012) Sources: Beckman, RlA 13 (2012)
Original script for Inaras: 𒀭𒄿𒈾𒊏 Script: Cuneiform (Hittite) Transliteration: ᵈi-na-ra (acc. ᵈi-na-ra-an) Steps: Written ᵈi-na-ra(-an) in the Illuyanka myth (CTH 321) Sources: CTH 321 (Illuyanka)

Original script for Ḫannaḫannas: 𒀭𒄩𒀭𒈾𒄩𒀭𒈾 Script: Cuneiform (Hittite) Transliteration: ᵈḫa-an-na-ḫa-an-na Steps: Written ᵈḫa-an-na-ḫa-an-na; a quoted cult text reads LÚSANGA ᵈḪa-an-na-ḫa-an-na (Kaskal 2024) Sources: Kaskal 2024 (Bo-Texte IV)

Original script for Kumarbiš: 𒀭𒆪𒈥𒁉 Script: Cuneiform (Hittite/Hurrian cycle) Transliteration: ᵈku-mar-bi (nom. ᵈku-mar-bi-iš) Steps: Written ᵈku-mar-bi(-iš) in the Song of Emergence (CTH 344): ᵈKu-mar-bi-iš A-la-lu-wa-aš… Sources: CTH 344 (Song of Emergence)

Original script for Alalu: 𒀭𒀀𒆷𒇻 Script: Cuneiform (Hittite/Hurrian cycle) Transliteration: ᵈa-la-lu (gen. ᵈa-la-lu-wa-aš) Steps: Written ᵈa-la-lu(-wa-aš) in the Song of Emergence (CTH 344) Sources: CTH 344 (Song of Emergence)

Original script for Ahriman: 𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎 Script: Avestan Transliteration: aŋra mainiiu Steps: Written aŋra mainiiu in the Avesta (Gathic nom. aŋrō mainiiuš, Yasna 45.2; Younger form at Vendidad 19.1) The Younger spelling writes the ending with two i-letters (…mainiiu) 'Ahriman' is the Middle Persian (Pahlavi) development of the same name Sources: Yasna 45.2, Vendidad 19.1

Original script for Ašavahišta: 𐬀𐬴𐬀 𐬬𐬀𐬵𐬌𐬱𐬙𐬀 Script: Avestan Transliteration: aṣ̌a vahišta Steps: Written aṣ̌a vahišta in the Avesta; the Aṣ̌əm Vohū prayer gives the oblique forms aṣ̌əm… vahištəm ṣ̌ is written 𐬴 (SSHE) and š 𐬱 (SHE) Sources: The Gathas (Amesha Spenta tradition), Aṣ̌əm Vohū prayer

Original script for Onuris: 𓏎𓈖𓁷𓂋𓏏𓈐𓅆 Script: Egyptian hieroglyphs Transliteration: ỉn-ḥrt Steps: Written ỉn-ḥrt, 'He who brings back the Distant One', the standard theonym of Thinis Greek rendered the name Ἀνουρις / Ὀνουρις, whence the modern form Onuris Sources: Standard theonym of Thinis (Greek Ἀνουρις)

Pronunciation of Apóllōn: /a.pól.lɔːn/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-POL-lone' — stress the second syllable and hold the final 'o' roughly twice as long as English allows. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: A-: Short alpha, smooth breathing — the name opens without roughness, like light arriving. -pól-: Pi plus acute on short omicron. The pitch peak falls on the second syllable, a rising call that carries across distance. -lōn: Lambda, long omega, nu. The long final vowel sustains and resolves the name like a held musical note. Note: Apóllōn is dual-tier because the Greek Ἀπόλλων carries both stress (acute on the second syllable) and length (omega in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Apóllōn with acute stress and Apollōn with macron-only length. Both forms are owned and both are philologically legitimate.

Pronunciation of Hádēs: /há.dɛːs/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'HAH-dace' — the first syllable is pitched high and sharp; the second is long and level, like the floor of the underworld. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ha-: Rough breathing on short alpha — the name expires outward, like a breath seen in cold air. -dēs: Delta plus long eta, the long vowel that opens the name into the unseen. Note: Hádēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἅιδης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name literally means 'the Unseen,' and the acute on the first syllable gives it the force of a warning.

Pronunciation of Hekátē: /he.ká.tɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'he-KAH-tay' — the second syllable rises in pitch, and the final 'ay' is held long like the 'a' in 'say' stretched out. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: He-: Rough breathing on short epsilon — the name begins with an audible exhalation, like a breath across a threshold. -ka-: Kappa plus acute on short alpha — the pitch peak, a sudden calling note. -tē: Long eta, the final syllable that draws the name into the dark. Note: Hekátē is dual-tier because the Greek Ἑκάτη carries both stress (acute on alpha) and length (eta in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Hekátē with acute stress and Hekatē with macron-only length. The form is etymologically debated, but both Unicode forms are orthographically legitimate.

Pronunciation of Níkē: /ní.kɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'NEE-kay' — the first syllable rises in pitch like a shout; the second is long and clear. Note: Níkē is dual-tier because the Greek Νίκη carries both stress (acute on the short ι) and length (long η), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Níkē with acute stress and Nikē with macron-only length. Both forms are owned and both preserve the goddess's essential meaning: Victory itself.

Pronunciation of Zeús: /zděu̯s/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ZDEWS' — one syllable, beginning with a buzzing 'zd' and ending in a sharp 's', like the sound of distant thunder compressed into a name. Note: Zeús is Tier 1 because the Greek Ζεύς contains both stress (acute on the diphthong ευ) and length (the diphthong itself counts as long for accentual purposes). The acute falls on the only syllable, making the name a single pitched peak — the sonic image of a thunderbolt.

Note: Árēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἄρης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name sounds like a wound being named: short, sharp, and final.

Pronunciation of Aphrodítē: /a.pʰro.dí.tɛː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-fro-DEE-tay' — the third syllable carries the pitch, and the final vowel is long and clear. Note: Aphrodítē is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀφροδίτη contains both stress (acute on the short iota) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name's foam etymology makes the long final vowel sound like a wave receding.

Pronunciation of Athēnâ: /a.tʰɛː́.naː/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-THAY-na' — the second syllable is pitched higher and drawn out; the final 'a' is long and pure. The restoration Athénā preserves the acute stress; Athēnā is the macron-only variant. The form Athēnē changes the final letter and is therefore used only when the domain requires it.

Pronunciation of Dēmētēr: /dɛ.mɛ́.tɛr/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'deh-MEH-ter' — stress the middle syllable; the final syllable is light and quick. Pronunciation of Poseidôn: /po.sei.dɔ́ːn/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'poh-SAY-done' — the second syllable is light, the third is long, pitched, and powerful. Pronunciation of Promētheús: /pro.mɛː.tʰeu̯s/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'pro-MAY-thyoos' — the middle syllable is long, and the final diphthong glides like the foresight the name denotes. Pronunciation of Cháos: /kʰá.os/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "KHAH-oss" — first syllable like "cat" with a breathy k, second like "oss" in "moss". Pronunciation of Tártaros: /tár.ta.ros/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: "TAR-ta-ross" — three syllables, the first pitched high like a stone dropping. The absence of long vowels makes the name sound hard and abrupt — the acoustic opposite of the bright, sustained Aithḗr.

Pronunciation of Árgos: /ár.gos/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'AR-goss' — two short syllables, stress forward, like a light snapping on. Note: Árgos is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄργος carries only the acute stress; both vowels are short, so a single feature separates the restoration from ASCII. The entry is the giant Argos Panoptes, Hera's hundred-eyed watcher — from ἀργός, 'shining, swift'. Reconstruction follows Allen, Vox Graeca; LSJ; and Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek.

Pronunciation of Mídas: /mí.das/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'MEE-dass' — stress forward, the first syllable bright and the second clipped; the English 'MY-das' flattens both. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Mí-: Bilabial nasal opening into acute-pitched iota [mí] — the name's single mark, pitched high. -d-: Voiced dental stop [d] — plain and firm. -as: Short alpha and final sigma [as] — the common ending of Anatolian royal names. Note: Mídas is Tier 2 because the Greek Μίδας carries only the acute stress; the vowels are short and no long vowel or diphthong is preserved. Behind the Greek form stands a genuine Phrygian royal name — Assyrian records know the same king as Mitâ of Muški. Reconstruction follows Allen, Vox Graeca; LSJ; and Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek.

Note: ʾAṯiratu is normalized [ʔaθ.i.ˈraː.tu]: glottal ʾalep, interdental ṯ (Greek theta), stress on the long penultimate ā, final short -u. The shorter form ʾAṯirat drops the final vowel. From ʾaṯr 'place, sanctuary'; her sea-epithet rbt ʾaṯrt ym, 'the Great Lady who walks on the Sea', underlies the Greek-era reading as a sea-goddess (Philo's Ἀσερά). Pronunciation of Baꜥal: /baʕ.al/ Label: Ugaritic/Phoenician Reconstruction Approximation: 'BAH-ahl' — the middle consonant is a deep, throaty 'ʿ' (like Arabic ع), not a glottal stop or silent letter. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: ba-: Plain voiced bilabial [b] plus open [a]; the word means 'lord, owner, husband' across Semitic languages. -ʕal: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] plus [a] and [l]. The pharyngeal is the signature consonant; we render it with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for registrability. Note: Baꜥal is technically a title ('Lord') that became a name. The ideal form includes Semitic ʿayin, which is blocked at the DNS root; the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) is the registrable compromise. The name is Tier 2 because it preserves the ʿayin as a distinctive phoneme but carries no stress or length mark. In texts he is often 'Baꜥlu-Haddu' or simply the 'Rider on the Clouds.'

Pronunciation of Ēl: /ʔeːl/ Label: Ugaritic/Phoenician Reconstruction Approximation: 'AYLE' — like 'ale' with a long vowel and a slight glottal catch at the beginning; the name is short and resonant. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: ʔē-: Glottal stop [ʔ] plus long [eː], marked by macron; the long vowel distinguishes the divine name from the common noun 'god' in some forms. -l: Voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l]; the root ʾil- means 'god, divine power' throughout Semitic. Note: Ēl is both a proper name and the common Semitic word for 'god.' The macron marks the long vowel inferred from Hebrew אֵל and Ugaritic spellings. As a Tier-2 name it preserves length (macron) but not stress/accent, fitting the project's convention for registering a single distinctive prosodic feature.

Pronunciation of ꜥAnat: /ʕa.nat/ Label: Ugaritic/Phoenician Reconstruction Approximation: 'AH-naht' — start with a rough, throaty 'ah' (like Arabic ع), then 'naht' with a crisp final t. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: ʕa-: Voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ] — a deep, tightening sound in the throat, followed by open [a]. The Egyptian Ain (ꜥ) is used as the registrable stand-in. -nat: Plain alveolar sounds: [n], [a], [t]. The final -t is a feminine marker, common in Semitic divine names. Note: The ideal spelling would use Semitic ʿayin (ʿ), but that character is rejected by the DNS root zone. We therefore render the pharyngeal with the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ, U+A724), the only registrable Unicode workaround that signals the original consonant. The name is Tier 2: it preserves the ʿayin (a distinctive phoneme) but lacks the long-vowel mark that would make it Tier 1.

Pronunciation of Ašeratu: /ʔa.ʃe.ˈra.tu/ Label: Canaanite/Phoenician Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-she-RAH-too' — begin with a slight catch in the throat, then 'she' with a crisp sh, roll or tap the r, and end with 'rah-too'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: ʔa-: Glottal stop [ʔ] followed by open [a]; the initial aleph of the Canaanite name (not a pharyngeal ʿayin, so the registrable form uses plain A). -še-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] plus mid front [e]. The š reflects the Phoenician/Canaanite sibilant; Ugaritic wrote the same consonant as ṯ (probably [θ]). -ra-: Tapped or trilled [r] plus open [a]. -tu: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] plus close back rounded vowel [u], the final nominative case vowel of the divine name in Ugaritic and Phoenician. Note: Reconstruction follows the Phoenician/Ugaritic nominative form ʾAšeratu. The initial consonant is a glottal stop (aleph), not a pharyngeal, so the PUNICODEX form uses plain A rather than Egyptological Ain. The medial š marks the Canaanite/Phoenician reflex of Proto-Semitic *ṯ, while Ugaritic retains the older ṯ (probably [θ]); the final -u is the case vowel, dropped in Hebrew Asherah. Tier 2: the caron on š preserves a distinctive Semitic phoneme, but there is no long-vowel or Greek-style stress feature. Sources: KTU, CIS/KAI, Smith The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Day Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan.

Pronunciation of Mūt: /moːt/ Label: Canaanite/Phoenician Reconstruction Approximation: 'MOHT' — one syllable with a long, drawn-out o (or oo) and a crisp final t. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: m: Voiced bilabial nasal [m]. ō: Long back-mid rounded vowel [oː]; the macron marks length only. The exact quality varies by dialect (Phoenician mūt, Hebrew māwet, Ugaritic mt is vowelless in writing). t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t], unaspirated. Note: The name is the Canaanite word for 'death.' The macron on the registrable Mōt signals vowel length, not a fixed quality: Phoenician has mūt, Hebrew māwet, and Ugaritic mt gives no vowels. We follow the PUNICODEX macron convention with /moːt/; hear a long low/back vowel rather than the short English 'o.' Tier 1: the macron preserves a reconstructed long vowel. Sources: KTU, CIS/KAI, Smith The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Day Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan.

Pronunciation of Ṛta: /r̩.tɐ/ Label: Sanskrit/Vedic Reconstruction Approximation: 'RIH-tuh' — the first syllable is a voiced r that carries the vowel, almost like 'rurr' clipped short; the t is crisp. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: Ṛ-: Syllabic retroflex r [r̩] — a vibrant, humming vowel unique to Sanskrit and its Indo-Iranian kin. -ta: Unaspirated [t] plus short [ɐ], a neutral ending that makes the abstract concrete: 'that which is'. Note: IAST Ṛta uses the underdotted ṛ for the syllabic r vowel. It is never personified in the Vedic corpus; it is the impersonal principle by which sun, moon, sacrifice, and morality all hold together. Devanagari ऋत is one of the most philosophically charged short words in Sanskrit.

Pronunciation of Bꜣ: /baːʕ/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'BAH-ah' — but close the final syllable with a soft catch in the throat, as if the name itself were a wing-beat. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: B-: Voiced bilabial stop [b], as in English 'bone' — the sound of manifestation taking shape. -aː-: Long open vowel reconstructed between the consonants; Egyptian hieroglyphs do not write vowels, so the length is inferred from Coptic and Semitic parallels. -ʕ: Final ꜣ (Egyptian alef), representing a voiced pharyngeal fricative or glottal catch — the breath that keeps the name open at the back of the throat. Note: Egyptian is written without vowels. The transliteration Bꜣ uses Gardiner's ꜣ (reversed glottal stop / alef) for the final guttural. The dot under ḥ in other entries marks a voiceless pharyngeal fricative; here the ꜣ marks a voiced counterpart or a glottal catch. The ba is Tier 2 in the PUNICODEX system because the restoration preserves one primary prosodic feature — the long vowel conventionally marked by the macron-less but historically long final syllable.

Pronunciation of Kꜣ: /kaːʔ/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'KAH-ah' — say a firm ka, hold the vowel, then close with a soft glottal catch. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: K-: Voiceless velar stop [k], the initial consonant of the life-force. -aː-: Long open vowel [aː], inferred from Coptic and from the word's prosodic weight. -ꜣ: Final Egyptological aleph [ʔ], a glottal catch that leaves the root open like a breath. Note: The ka is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves the long vowel and final Egyptological aleph (ꜣ) as distinctive features, without a Greek-style stress mark. Egyptian vowels are not written in hieroglyphs and must be reconstructed.

Pronunciation of ꜥAsherah: /ʔa.ʃeː.ra/ Label: Ugaritic/Phoenician Reconstruction Approximation: 'ah-SHAY-rah' — start with a slight catch in the throat, then a long 'shay' and a soft 'rah'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: ʔa-: Glottal stop [ʔ] followed by open [a]; in some reconstructions the initial consonant is a pharyngeal ʿ rather than a glottal stop. The Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) marks this debated point. -šē-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] plus long [eː], marked by macron; the length is inferred from Hebrew and Aramaic reflexes. -ra: Tapped or trilled [r] plus final [a], a feminine ending. Note: The initial consonant of the Ugaritic name is disputed: some read it as a glottal stop (ʾ), others as a pharyngeal (ʿ). We follow the lexicon's use of Egyptian Ain (ꜥ) as the registrable compromise. The long ē is marked with a macron to preserve the length implied by Hebrew and Aramaic cognates; stress falls on the long middle syllable.

Pronunciation of Ōkeanós: /o.ke.a.nós/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'oh-keh-ah-NOSS' — the final syllable carries the pitch, like the river returning to itself. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: O-: Short omicron — the name begins with the round sound of water. -ke-: Kappa plus short epsilon — the compact middle. -a-: Short alpha — the open central vowel. -nós: Nu plus acute on short omicron — the stressed peak that names the encircling river. Note: Ōkeanos is Tier 2 because the Greek Ὠκεανός preserves stress (acute on the short ό) but no long vowel in our registrable restoration. The initial omega is long, but the acute falls on the final omicron. The ideal form Ōkeanós is difficult to register; Okeanos is the standard form used here.

Pronunciation of Trengtreng: /tɾeŋˈtɾeŋ/ Label: Mapudungun Reconstruction Approximation: TRENG-TRENG — a rattling, drum-like reduplication that mimics successive thunderclaps. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: tɾeŋ: Alveolar onset followed by close-mid [e] and a velar nasal [ŋ]; the first syllable of the reduplicated thunder name. -: Reduplication divider; the name is doubled to intensify sound and power. tɾeŋ: Repeated syllable, producing the rattling, drum-like effect of rolling thunder. Note: Trengtreng is a reduplicated, onomatopoeic Mapuche name for thunder; reduplication is a productive device for intensification in Mapudungun. Because the Latin alphabet renders all of its sounds without diacritics, the Unicode restoration coincides with the ASCII form, so the name is Tier 2 by tradition rather than by restored marks.

Pronunciation of Aša: /aʃa/ Label: Avestan Reconstruction Approximation: "AH-shah" — two level syllables, with a crisp "sh" in the middle and no stress thrown onto either vowel. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: a-: Open unrounded vowel [a], the first breath of the name — short, clear, and level. -š-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ], like English "sh" but sharper; the caron marks the sound that separates Avestan from ordinary "sa". -a: Final open vowel [a], equal in weight to the first; Avestan vowel quantity is real, and the name balances on the two. Note: Aša is Tier 2 because the registrable form Aša preserves the postalveolar š (caron) but carries no stress or length mark. The Avestan original was likely pronounced with a level or slightly rising pitch on an open [a], but standard scholarly transliteration does not encode Avestan accent. The š is not decorative: it distinguishes the name from ordinary "asa" and points back to the Avestan letter 𐬴 (še).

Pronunciation of Vāc: /ʋaːtʃ/ Label: Vedic Sanskrit Reconstruction Approximation: "VAHCH" — one long syllable, like "watch" but with the vowel drawn out and a crisper final "ch." Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: V-: Labiodental approximant [ʋ], softer than English v; the lips almost meet but do not buzz. -ā-: Long open back vowel [aː], held roughly twice the length of short a; the macron is the vowel's length, not stress. -c: Voiceless palatal affricate [tɕ] or [tʃ], like English "ch" but more forward on the palate; the virāma marks that no vowel follows. Note: Vāc is Tier 2 because the registrable form Vāc preserves the long ā (macron) but carries no stress mark. Vedic Sanskrit was pitch-accented, but the position of the accent in Vāc is not normally encoded in transliteration. The virāma on the Devanagari च् indicates the consonant is final, making the name a single closed syllable: vāc.

Pronunciation of Hén: /hɛ́n/ Label: Attic Greek Reconstruction Approximation: 'HEN' — with a slight initial h and a rising pitch on the first, only syllable. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: h-: Rough breathing [h], the audible breath that precedes the vowel in classical Greek. -é-: Short epsilon with acute pitch stress [ɛ́], the prosodic peak of the word. -n: Voiced alveolar nasal [n], closing the syllable. Note: Hén is Tier 2: the Greek ἕν preserves only the acute pitch stress on the first syllable and has no long vowel. It is an Accent-Preserving Tier-2 name.

Pronunciation of Liwyāṯān: /liwjaːˈθaːn/ Label: Biblical Hebrew (Tiberian/Masoretic) Approximation: 'liw-yah-THAHN' — 'liw' rhymes with 'live'; the middle 'yah' is long and stressed; the final 'th' is soft as in 'think', and the last 'a' is drawn out. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: li-: Alveolar lateral [l] followed by short [i], the hireq under ל. -wə-: Labio-velar approximant [w], the waw functioning as a consonant, with a short vocal sheva [ə]. -yā-: Palatal approximant [j], the yod functioning as a consonant, followed by long [ɔː], the qamets gadol under י. -ṯān: Voiceless interdental fricative [θ] — spirantized taw without dagesh — plus long [ɔː], the qamets gadol under ת, and final [n]. Note: BHS points the name לִוְיָתָן (Job 3:8). The form is a nominal derivative from l-w-h 'to twist, turn' with the -ān suffix; the medial waw and yod are consonantal, yielding the sequence [liwjaː-]. Both qamets vowels are long [ɔː]. The taw lacks dagesh and is therefore spirantized [θ] in the Tiberian tradition. The Ugaritic cognate ltn (KTU 1.5 i 1–3) is vocalized by scholars as /lītan-/ or /lōtanu/. HALOT s.v. לִוְיָתָן; TDOT s.v. Leviathan; Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, 105–6.

Pronunciation of Nḫt: /ˈnaxt/ Label: Egyptological Reconstruction Approximation: 'NAKHT' — one syllable, with the 'kh' like Scottish 'loch' (not 'k'). Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: N-: Alveolar nasal [n], as in English 'no'. -a-: Short open vowel; Egyptian hieroglyphs do not write vowels, so the vowel quality is inferred from Coptic and from Semitic transcriptions. -ḫ-: Voiceless velar fricative [x], like the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'; written with h-breve (U+1E2B). -t: Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the final consonant of the root. Note: The Egyptian root nḫt means 'strong, mighty, victorious'. Hieroglyphs record only N-ḫ-t; the vowel is reconstructed from Coptic ⲛⲟϭ and from the pattern of Egyptian triliteral nouns. The ḫ is a voiceless velar fricative. In PUNICODEX the Nḫt spelling uses the registrable h-breve (U+1E2B) as a Tier 2 restoration; the ASCII fallback is 'nakht'. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014); Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. nḫt; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache II, s.v. nḫt; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on Egyptian ḫ in Semitic orthography.

Pronunciation of Mōšeh: /moːˈʃɛh/ Label: Biblical Hebrew (Tiberian/Masoretic) Approximation: 'moh-SHEH' — the first vowel is long and steady like 'mow'; the second syllable is short and crisp, ending in a soft breath. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: mō-: Bilabial nasal [m] followed by long [oː], the Tiberian holam under מ. -šeh: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — Hebrew shin, marked by the upper right dot — plus short [ɛ], the segol under ש; the final ה is silent in Masoretic reading, often transcribed only as a breath. Note: BHS points the name מֹשֶׁה (Exodus 2:10). The first vowel is a long holam [oː]; the second is a short segol [ɛ]. The Tiberian tradition preserves the final he as a silent mater, not as a pronounced consonant. The name lacks the Tiberian pharyngeals aleph [ʔ] and ayin [ʕ]. HALOT s.v. מֹשֶׁה; TDOT s.v. Moses; Khan, The Tiberian Pronunciation Tradition of Biblical Hebrew (2020).

Pronunciation of Dāwîḏ: /dɔːˈwiːð/ Label: Biblical Hebrew (Tiberian/Masoretic) Approximation: 'daw-EEDH' — draw out the first 'aw' like 'dawn'; the middle sound is 'wee' with a glide; the final consonant is a soft 'th' as in 'this'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: dā-: Voiced alveolar plosive [d] — dalet with dagesh — followed by long [ɔː], the qamets gadol under ד. -wî-: Labio-velar approximant [w], the waw functioning as a consonant, plus long [iː] from the hireq-yod combination. -ḏ: Voiced dental fricative [ð] — spirantized dalet without dagesh. Some reading traditions keep the final consonant plosive [d], so the exact realization is uncertain. Note: BHS points the royal name דָּוִד (1 Samuel 16:13). The initial dalet carries a dagesh (plosive [d]) and a long qamets [ɔː]; the medial waw functions as a consonant [w] with hireq [iː]; the final dalet is spirantized [ð] in Tiberian because it lacks dagesh, though the phonetic realization of a final fricative is debated. HALOT s.v. דָּוִד; TDOT s.v. David.

Pronunciation of Šəlōmōh: /ʃəloːˈmoː(h)/ Label: Biblical Hebrew (Tiberian/Masoretic) Approximation: 'shuh-LOH-moh' — start with a quick 'shuh'; both later 'o' sounds are long and steady, like 'show'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: šə-: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] — Hebrew shin, marked by the upper right dot — with a short vocal sheva [ə]. -lō-: Lateral approximant [l] followed by long [oː], the holam under ל. -mō(h): Bilabial nasal [m] plus long [oː], the holam under מ; the final ה is silent, a mater lectionis for the long vowel. Note: BHS points the name שְׁלֹמֹה (1 Kings 1:1). The initial shewa is vocal (šəwa naʿ) because it opens the word; the two holams are long [oː]. The final he is silent. Modern Israeli Hebrew flattens the vowels to [o] and often elides the shewa, but the Tiberian tradition distinguishes length. HALOT s.v. שְׁלֹמֹה; TDOT s.v. Solomon.

Pronunciation of Nōaḥ: /ˈnoːaħ/ Label: Biblical Hebrew (Tiberian/Masoretic) Approximation: 'NOH-ahkh' — stress the first syllable and hold the 'o'; the final syllable is a quick 'ah' followed by a throaty 'kh' as in Scottish 'loch'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: nō-: Alveolar nasal [n] followed by long [oː], the holam under נ. -aḥ: Short [a] from the furtive patah, pronounced before the final voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ] — Hebrew ḥet. Some traditions render ḥet as a uvular [χ]. Note: BHS points the name נֹחַ (Genesis 5:29). The patah under the final ḥet is a furtive patah (pataḥ ganuv): it is pronounced as a short [a] before the guttural, and the word stress remains on the long holam (hence 'NOH-ahkh', not 'no-AHKH'). The ḥet is a voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ] in Tiberian, though Modern Hebrew merges it with [χ]. HALOT s.v. נֹחַ; TDOT s.v. Noah.

Pronunciation of Qāyīn: /qaˈjiːn/ Label: Biblical Hebrew (Tiberian/Masoretic) Approximation: 'kah-YEEN' — the first consonant is a deep 'k' made at the back of the throat (like Arabic qāf); the second syllable is a long 'yeen'. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: qa-: Voiceless uvular plosive [q] — Hebrew qof — followed by short [a], the patah under ק. -yīn: Palatal approximant [j], the yod as consonant, plus long [iː] from the hireq-yod combination, ending in alveolar nasal [n]. Note: BHS points the name קַיִן (Genesis 4:1). The first vowel is a short patah [a] in the Masoretic pointing, although the qāṭīl-pattern form historically had a long *ā (reflected in the PUNICODEX macron convention Qāyīn); the second vowel is a long hireq-yod [iː]. The qof is a uvular [q], distinct from kaf. HALOT s.v. קַיִן; TDOT s.v. Cain.

Pronunciation of Hāḇel: /ˈhɛvɛl/ Label: Biblical Hebrew (Tiberian/Masoretic) Approximation: 'HEH-vel' — both vowels are short 'e' as in 'bed'; the 'v' is soft, and the stress falls on the first syllable. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: hĕ-: Voiceless glottal fricative [h] — Hebrew he — followed by short [ɛ], the segol under ה. -vel: Voiced labiodental fricative [v] — Hebrew vet without dagesh, fricative [β]/[v] — plus short [ɛ], the segol under ב, ending in [l]. Note: BHS points the name הֶבֶל (Genesis 4:2). The Tiberian/Masoretic pronunciation is Hevel [ˈhɛvɛl], with two short segol vowels and a fricative bet (vet). The PUNICODEX display form Hāḇel follows the Greek/Latin conventional spelling (Ἅβελ / Abel) rather than the Masoretic vocalization; the macron on ā is not supported by the Tiberian pointing. HALOT s.v. הֶבֶל; TDOT s.v. Abel.

Pronunciation of Lóng: /lʊŋ˧˥/ Label: Modern Standard Mandarin (Pinyin) Approximation: LUHNG — the 'o' is like the 'oo' in 'book', and the tone rises from mid to high, as in a questioning intonation. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: lóng: Single syllable with voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l], final [ʊŋ] (close-mid back rounded vowel + velar nasal), and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'o' before 'ng' corresponds to IPA [ʊ]. Note: 龍 denotes the Chinese dragon, an emblem of imperial authority, fertility, and cosmic yang force. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is lóng (Tone 2), as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese form as *[m]-roŋ (GSR 1193a). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Lóng preserves the citation rising tone of the second tone; in connected speech the contour may be compressed, but the lexical tone remains Tone 2.

Pronunciation of Wújí: /u˧˥ tɕi˧˥/ Label: Modern Standard Mandarin (Pinyin) Approximation: WOO-JEE — both syllables carry a rising tone (mid to high), like a gentle question on each half. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: wú: Syllable beginning with labio-velar glide [w] (written 'w' in Pinyin), high back rounded vowel [u], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). jí: Syllable with unaspirated alveolo-palatal affricate [tɕ], high front vowel [i], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'j' is always [tɕ] before front vowels. Note: 無極 (Wújí) means 'Limitless' or 'Ultimate Nothing', the undifferentiated state before the emergence of Tàijí in Zhou Dunyi's Taijitu shuo. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is wú (Tone 2) + jí (Tone 2), per the Hanyu Pinyin scheme and the Unihan Database (kMandarin). Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 無 as *ma (GSR 0103a, 'not have') and 極 as *[g](r)ək (GSR 0910e, 'extreme'). The Unicode restoration Wújí preserves the parallel rising tones of both syllables.

Pronunciation of Yīnyáng: /in˥ jaŋ˧˥/ Label: Modern Standard Mandarin (Pinyin) Approximation: YIN-YAHNG — first syllable high and level, second syllable rising from mid to high. Dialect: Confidence: canonical Phonemes: yīn: Syllable with high front glide [j] (written 'y' in Pinyin), high front vowel [i], alveolar nasal [n], and Tone 1 (high level, ˥). yáng: Syllable with glide [j], open vowel [a], velar nasal [ŋ], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). The final '-ng' is a single velar nasal, not a cluster. Note: 陰陽 (Yīnyáng) denotes the complementary cosmic dualities—dark/passive/female and bright/active/male—central to Daoist cosmology, traditional Chinese medicine, and the Yijing. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is yīn (Tone 1) + yáng (Tone 2), as given in the Unihan Database (kMandarin). For historical context, Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 陰 as *q(r)um (GSR 0651y, 'dark') and 陽 as *laŋ (GSR 0720e, 'bright'). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Yīnyáng accurately preserves the citation tones.
